hints: Think about what severe diarrhoea actually removes from the body and why that loss is life-threatening.
Recall the simple home-made drink given for any diarrhoeal disease that replaces both water and solutes to allow absorption in the intestine.
walkthrough:
Why dehydration is the killer**
Cholera toxin causes massive loss of water and ions from the intestine in watery diarrhoea. Without replacement, blood volume falls and cells cannot function normally.

What the standard home treatment replaces**
Give oral rehydration solution - clean water containing dissolved glucose and salts such as sodium, potassium and chloride. Glucose helps co-transport of sodium and water back into blood from the intestine, so fluid is replaced quickly.
Final answer: Oral rehydration salts / solution / therapy; a solution of water with glucose and salts (e.g. sodium, potassium, chloride, citrate).

hints: Think beyond helping the one patient - if they get better faster, what happens to the time they are producing infective diarrhoea?
Link diarrhoea containing bacteria to the main route of cholera spread through contaminated water.
walkthrough:
Faster recovery means less shedding**
Rehydrated patients recover more quickly and produce diarrhoea for a shorter time. That diarrhoea contains live Vibrio cholerae.

Break the faecal-oral transmission chain**
Less diarrhoea for less time means less chance of bacteria contaminating drinking water. With less contamination, fewer new people are infected, so a large epidemic is less likely.
Final answer: Decreases recovery time / stops diarrhoea sooner; so less pathogen shed in faeces to contaminate water, reducing transmission to others.

hints: Focus on the tip of the Y-shaped antibody where the antigen actually fits - what is special about that region in each monoclonal antibody?
Think about protein structure and shape matching, like a lock and key, between that tip and only one antigen.
walkthrough:
Different sequence gives different shape**
All antibodies share the same basic Y shape, but each monoclonal antibody has its own specific amino acid sequence in the variable regions. This folds into a unique tertiary structure at the antigen-binding sites.

Complementary fit allows only one antigen**
The binding site is complementary in shape and charge to only one specific antigen, O1 or O139. Only that Vibrio antigen can fit and bind, so anti-O1 will not bind O139 antigen and vice versa.

Final answer: Each mAb has specific antigen-binding sites with specific variable region / amino acid sequence / tertiary structure; binding site and antigen have complementary shapes so only specific antigen binds.

hints: Start by checking area 4 on both strips - what does a coloured band there tell you about whether you can trust the test?
Compare areas 2 and 3 for person A versus person B to see which strain-specific line has appeared.
Trace the journey of the sample from area 1 upwards to explain why a trapped gold-labelled complex makes a visible band only where its matching antigen is present.
walkthrough:
Check the control first**
Both person A and person B show a coloured band at area 4. That confirms the mixture flowed correctly and the strips are working, so the test results are valid.

Read person A - O1 positive**
Person A has bands at 4 and at 3, but none at 2. In area 1 the mobile anti-O1 antibody attached to gold particles has bound O1 antigen from the faecal sample to form an antigen-antibody complex. Carried up to area 3, this complex is trapped by the immobilised antibody that binds complex O1, concentrating gold particles to give a visible coloured band. No O139 antigen is present, so nothing is trapped at area 2.

Read person B - negative**
Person B has only the control band at 4, with no colour at 2 or 3. There is no Vibrio O1 or O139 antigen in the sample, so no mobile antibody-antigen complexes form in area 1 and nothing is trapped at areas 2 or 3. Person B does not have cholera O1 or O139.

Final answer: Both tests valid as control area 4 shows band; person A is infected with V. cholerae O1 - band in area 3 due to mobile anti-O1 binding O1 antigen then complex binding to immobilised antibody in area 3; person B does not have cholera - no bands in areas 2 and 3 as no antigen so no antigen-antibody complexes formed and trapped.

hints: Identify the correct row for people who truly have cholera by culture, then divide those correctly found by the dipstick by the total truly positive.
walkthrough:
Use only the true cholera cases**
Culture shows 102 positive results for cholera. Of these, the dipstick correctly diagnosed 97. Calculate $\frac{97}{102} \times 100 = 95.098...\%$, about $95.1\%$.

hints: Compare growing bacteria for days in a lab with dipping a strip in a sample - think about time, place and labour.
walkthrough:
Why a dipstick suits an outbreak**
Culture needs an equipped laboratory and incubation time. A dipstick gives a visible result in minutes, is portable, needs only one person, and can be used in the field or village to test many people quickly.
Final answer: Quicker to obtain result / less time-consuming; or can be used in wider variety of places / portable / easier to test many people at once / less labour intensive.
